issues.legal_issue: An Under Secretary may sign a land-acquisition declaration when the applicable rules authorize that officer to authenticate government orders.
material_facts: The land-acquisition declarations were signed by an Under Secretary and expressed to be made in the name of the Governor.
The applicable Rules of Business authorized an Under Secretary, among other listed officers, to sign and authenticate government orders and instruments.
issues.conclusion: The Under Secretary was competent to sign the declarations; no separate special authorization under the Land Acquisition Act was required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits a declaration to be signed by a Secretary or an officer duly authorized to certify government orders. The Act and the General Clauses Act do not define “Secretary” to exclude an Under Secretary. Rule 13 of the Rules of Business made under Article 166 of the Constitution authorizes an Under Secretary to authenticate government orders, which is sufficient authority for this purpose.

predicates.land_acquisition_declaration: The proceeding involved a government declaration identifying land for acquisition.
predicates.signer_is_under_secretary: An Under Secretary signed the declaration.

issues.definition: When an Under Secretary signs a government land-acquisition declaration, the Under Secretary is competent to sign it.

issues.legal_issue: A bare allegation that the government did not form the required opinion does not, by itself, raise a factual issue about the validity of a properly expressed and authenticated executive order.
material_facts: The executive action was expressed in the name of the Governor and the orders were authenticated in the manner prescribed by the Rules of Business.
The original petitions asserted that the government had not formed the necessary opinion but did not allege supporting facts establishing that claim.
The government later filed affidavits describing how the decisions had been made.
issues.conclusion: The properly expressed and authenticated orders attracted the presumption of regularity, and the bare assertion did not require the government to prove that it had formed the required opinion.
issues.legal_principle: Article 166(2) prevents the validity of an order authenticated as prescribed from being challenged on the ground that it was not made or executed by the Governor. The Court also applied the presumption of regularity of official acts and held that a bare denial of the government’s opinion, without definite supporting facts, did not raise an issue requiring an answer.

rule.if: government_order_challenge and order_expressed_in_governor_name and order_properly_authenticated and allegation_lacks_supporting_facts

predicates.government_order_challenge: A person challenged the validity of a government order in a proceeding concerning land acquisition.
predicates.order_expressed_in_governor_name: The executive action was expressed to be taken in the Governor’s name.
predicates.order_properly_authenticated: The order was authenticated in the prescribed manner.
predicates.allegation_lacks_supporting_facts: The challenger asserted that the government had not formed the required opinion without alleging definite supporting facts.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a government order, a properly expressed and authenticated order coupled with an unsupported allegation that no opinion was formed does not make that allegation a factual issue requiring an answer.

issues.legal_issue: The government may authorize departmental secretaries to determine whether the urgency procedure applies, and that authorization need not be made by a standing order or in writing.
material_facts: The Minister arranged for the departmental secretaries to take action on urgent land acquisitions and instructed them that relevant cases could be handled without being brought to the Minister personally.
The secretaries and other departmental officers were authorized to take the necessary action and assessed the urgency and nature of the land before applying the urgency procedure.
The Rules of Business and instructions permitted the Minister to arrange with the Secretary which matters or classes of matters were to be brought to the Minister’s personal notice.
The Rules and instructions did not require the relevant arrangement to be in writing or made by standing order.
issues.conclusion: The secretaries’ determinations were determinations of the government, and the directions applying the urgency procedure were not invalid for want of written instructions or standing orders.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 7, 10, 13 and 15 of the Rules of Business, together with paragraphs 3 and 4 of the Governor’s instructions, permit the Minister to arrange with the Secretary which matters or classes of matters need personal attention. Standing orders concern the disposal of cases generally; an arrangement concerning particular matters arising within a case may be made without a standing order. The Court distinguished Emperor v. Shibnath Banerji, L.R. 72 I.A. 241, because there the official had not independently considered the matter as required. It referred to Shayamaghana Ray v. State, A.I.R. 1952 Orissa 230, in considering the instructions supplementing the Rules.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The government was acquiring land through a procedure that permitted action on grounds of urgency.
predicates.minister_arranged_delegation_of_matter: The responsible Minister arranged for departmental officers to handle the relevant matter without referring each instance for personal attention.
predicates.departmental_officers_assessed_urgency_a: The departmental officers considered whether urgency existed and whether the land met the relevant character requirement.

issues.definition: In an urgent land-acquisition proceeding, when the Minister arranges for departmental officers to handle the matter and those officers assess the relevant conditions, their determination is the government’s determination.

issues.legal_issue: Land actually under cultivation is arable land for the purpose of the urgency possession procedure.
material_facts: The land at issue was under cultivation.
The acquisition proceeded under the statutory urgency procedure, which permitted early possession of waste or arable land.
The Act provided for compensation for standing crops and trees on land taken under the urgency procedure.
issues.conclusion: Arable land includes land actually under cultivation as well as land capable of cultivation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted section 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, including section 17(3), which provides for compensation for standing crops and trees. The reference to crops shows that arable land may be cultivated or fallow; land on which crops are grown is not excluded from being arable. The Court approved Baldeo Singh v. State of U.P., A.I.R. 1965 All. 433, Smt. Lakshmi Devi v. State of Bihar, A.I.R. 1965 Pat. 400, and Guntur Ramalakshmamma v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, A.I.R. 1967 A.P. 280, and overruled Sadruddin Suleman v. J.H. Patwardhan, A.I.R. 1965 Bom. 224.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerned acquisition of land under a procedure allowing early possession of land of a specified kind.
predicates.land_actually_cultivated: The land was actually being cultivated.
predicates.land_fit_for_cultivation: The land was capable of or fit for cultivation.

issues.definition: In an urgent land-acquisition proceeding, land is arable if it is actually cultivated or fit for cultivation.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory provisions permitting early possession of qualifying land in urgent cases and dispensing with the ordinary objection process are not unconstitutional.
material_facts: The acquisition used the statutory urgency procedure, including the direction that the ordinary objection process would not apply and the direction permitting early possession of qualifying land.
The challengers argued that the provisions authorizing those steps violated constitutional protections concerning equality and property.
issues.conclusion: The provisions were not unconstitutional, and the constitutional challenge failed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the challenge to sections 17(1) and 17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, under Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, stating that the High Court’s judgment adequately answered the objections.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding involved use of statutory powers for urgent land acquisition.
predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_urgency_powe: A challenger argued that the powers used in the urgency procedure violated constitutional protections.

issues.definition: When statutory urgency powers are used in a land-acquisition proceeding and their constitutionality is challenged, the ruling is that those powers are not unconstitutional.
